data.title: AI Demand Will Keep DRAM Market Under Pressure
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The seemingly unending surge in AI infrastructure spending will continue to create DRAM supply shortages, which industry analysts believe could persist well into 2027 and potentially beyond.

This latest cycle differs significantly from previous DRAM booms and busts, when memory demand was tied largely to PCs and smartphones. AI has made memory a critical component of data center infrastructure, leading to more acute and long-lasting supply constraints.

“This is the most undersupplied the DRAM market has been in decades,” Mike Howard, director of DRAM and memory markets at TechInsights, said in an interview with EE Times, adding that pricing and revenue growth have surged as AI deployments accelerate. He expects supply constraints to continue through 2027 because demand growth is exceeding the industry’s ability to add manufacturing capacity.

Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, shares a similar view. “I don’t see how markets really loosen up anytime soon,” he said in an interview with EE Times. “Everybody knows that the capacity that comes in next year seems to be fully committed, so I don’t see a scenario where you have excess supply in the next 18 months.”

Despite the high demand, memory makers are exercising discipline. Rather than overbuilding capacity as they have in previous cycles—which ultimately led to significant oversupply and collapsing prices—they are taking a more measured approach. “They’ve been very methodical and very careful to spend money because of what’s happened cycle after cycle,” Gastwirth said.

He pointed to long-term agreements and customer-funded expansion plans as evidence that producers are growing capacity with considerably less risk than in the past.

Howard also sees structural changes reducing the likelihood of a classic memory crash. Long-term supply agreements now cover a significant portion of industry output, helping suppliers better align production with demand and avoid large inventory accumulations.

What remains to be seen is whether the current AI demand can remain strong enough over the longer term to justify continued expansion and whether the AI bubble is on the verge of popping.

Both Howard and Gastwirth expect the long-term trajectory to maintain its course, regardless of any setbacks. “There is real concern about an AI bust, and it is warranted,” Howard said. However, the economic promise of AI and the need for increasingly capable computing systems support ongoing investment, he said.

Gastwirth said he doesn’t believe there will be an AI bust given all the benefits that have already been seen from LLMs alone. He acknowledged uncertainty around issues such as job displacement and adoption timelines, but he believes AI’s impact is already too significant to reverse.

Beyond training and inference workloads, Gastwirth sees robotics and physical AI as the next major driver of memory demand. “When you get the robotics really starting to pick up, you need duplicate and triplicate systems for robots to really work.” He said the amount of information that’s gathered with all the sensors will require exponentially more DRAM.

Gastwirth said the resulting data growth from physical AI could create new demand streams that extend the current memory cycle well beyond today’s data center buildouts.

“Memory has become one of the most important components in the AI hardware stack, often the gating semiconductor component,” Howard said, arguing that memory now serves as a bottleneck for system deployment rather than a supporting element.

The consequences are already being felt outside the AI market. With hyperscale customers willing to pay premium prices for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM, consumer electronics makers find themselves lower on suppliers’ priority lists.

Gastwirth said he expects higher component costs to translate into fewer consumer products and increased prices as memory can account for roughly 30% of a product’s bill of materials, making shortages particularly painful for consumer device makers.

Both analysts agree that AI customers will continue receiving preferential treatment as long as supply remains constrained. Howard estimates that AI-related applications could account for as much as 75% of total DRAM revenue within a few years.

Howard and Gastwirth aren’t the only analysts singing from the same songbook.

According to a recently published report by Dell’Oro Group, worldwide data center IT semiconductor and component revenue for servers and storage systems surged 182% in the second quarter of 2026, with DRAM and storage revenue growing at a triple-digit pace, as average selling prices per bit more than doubled year over year. Accelerated server deployments also drove strong demand for complementary components, including HBM, CPUs, memory, and high-speed back-end NICs.

Omdia has also raised its 2026 semiconductor revenue forecast to 94.1% year-over-year growth, driven by unprecedented demand for DRAM as AI infrastructure investment continues to outpace global supply, with memory ICs now expected to account for more than 50% of total semiconductor revenue in 2026.

The research firm said AI demand has exceeded the industry’s current ability to produce and package chips, with bottlenecks across HBM, advanced packaging, and node capacity expected to persist until at least 2027.

data.title: Piecing Together the Indian Electronics and Semiconductor Ecosystem
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

India’s electronics ecosystem is assembling itself like a puzzle, with stubborn pieces trying to find their place—some already locked in, many still being cut to shape.

When S. Krishnan, secretary of the Indian Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, called 2026 a “landmark year” for semiconductors, he wasn’t pointing only to the ₹1.275 trillion (~$13.25 billion) outlay under India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 (ISM 2.0). He was also pointing to three semiconductor packaging facilities set up by Micron, Kaynes, and CG Semi in Sanand, Gujarat, which began commercial production in the first half of 2026—proof that some pieces have already clicked into place. However, locking a piece in place doesn’t mean the puzzle is solved. These packaging units run on legacy processes—the harder climb toward flip-chip, 2.5D, and DRAM packaging is still ahead.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi framed the ambition in sweeping terms at the inauguration of CG Semi’s commercial production: “Our aim is to develop the entire ecosystem in India, from chip design to fabrication to packaging. … India’s youth will drive the next technological revolution—in AI, robotics, and next-gen tech—powered by Made in India chips.”

It’s a compelling vision, but most of the equipment and specialty chemicals feeding India’s electronics and semiconductor ecosystem are still imported. That remains a structural vulnerability that undercuts the “self-reliance” messaging until the upstream capabilities—materials, equipment, and process technology—that ISM 2.0 promises are actually built.

That’s precisely where the smaller, sharper pieces—India’s deep-tech startups—earn their place. Vimag Labs is building a wirelessly excited motor that needs no rare-Earth magnets. NoPo Technologies is scaling single-walled carbon nanotube production for electronics and energy storage, building what it claims will be the world’s second-largest such plant in Bengaluru and going head-to-head with established global manufacturers.

If you think the puzzle ends at motors and materials, take a breath: India is also reaching for compute itself. Amith Singhee, CTO of IBM India and South Asia, walked through the company’s planned Quantum System Two installation in Amaravati, which is set to put a production-grade quantum computer within reach of Indian researchers. Meanwhile, researchers at IIT Bombay and IISc Bangalore are working on neuromorphic chips wired to think the way brains do.

In this Special Report, EE Times lays out every piece as it’s cut and placed—the packaging plants racing toward advanced nodes, the startups rewriting India’s supply chain, and the labs betting on compute architectures the world hasn’t commercialized yet.

India Moves to Close Gaps in Its Electronics Supply Chain

India races to own more of its electronics value chain, from OSATs to PCBs, but imported materials still hold the leash.

India’s OSAT-ATMP Build-Out: From Legacy Packages to 2.5D

ASIP Technologies has begun construction of an OSAT facility in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, with Korean partner APACT.

India’s Quantum Journey Goes Beyond the Qubit

IBM’s Amaravati deployment could accelerate India’s quantum ecosystem as startups develop processors, software, and supporting technologies.

Indian Researchers Look Beyond GPUs to Neuromorphic AI Hardware

As AI workloads become more computationally demanding, Indian researchers argue that the next advance may come from rethinking computing architecture itself.

Indian Firm Scales Single-Walled Carbon Nanotube Production for Batteries and Chips

NoPo scales HiPco single-walled carbon nanotube output for sub-2-nm chips and anodes.

Indian Startup Vimag Labs Develops Wirelessly Excited Motor Without Rare-Earth Magnets

Vimag Labs ditches rare-earth magnets with a wirelessly excited EV motor claiming PMSM-level punch.

data.title: U.S. Awards Anderon $1B for Quantum Wafer Manufacturing
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Anderon, IBM’s new quantum chip foundry, announced this week that it will receive a $1 billion CHIPS Act award from the U.S. Department of Commerce to accelerate U.S. quantum wafer production. The timing of the investment comes as quantum computing transitions from lab experiments toward production scale, one analyst told EE Times.

Headquartered in Albany, New York, Anderon makes 300-mm quantum wafers for parent IBM and other customers that the company declined to identify. Late last year, IBM said it is in a dead heat with Google to win the quantum advantage race within months. IBM expects to release its Starling quantum computer to customers in 2029.

“IBM’s quantum roadmap requires a manufacturing foundation that can scale at the pace our work demands,” Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, said in the announcement. “Anderon’s focus on wafer fabrication gives us exactly that and strengthens our ability to execute and accelerate progress toward the next era of quantum computing.”

In the near term, quantum computing promises to aid in discoveries of advanced materials and chemicals that have been beyond the reach of existing computing power. Other quantum technologies such as sensing are gaining traction.

Anderon joins companies such as SkyWater and GlobalFoundries entering the quantum foundry business. SkyWater’s quantum chip customers include IonQ, Qolab, and PsiQuantum. IonQ completed its acquisition of SkyWater in July. GlobalFoundries customers include PsiQuantum, Quantinuum, and Diraq.

Since the beginning of 2026, there have been multiple acquisitions and funding announcements involving quantum foundries with different manufacturing approaches worldwide. They include Anderon, GlobalFoundries, SkyWater, Quantum Computing, and Quantum Foundry Copenhagen, Heather West, IDC’s quantum research lead, told EE Times.

“That diversity is important because quantum chip manufacturing is not simply a matter of moving a quantum design into a conventional semiconductor fab,” West said. “Quantum devices can require specialized process flows, materials, metrology, packaging, and yield optimization that a traditional semiconductor foundry may not have developed. At the same time, quantum has long R&D cycles and relatively low volumes, which makes it difficult for any single manufacturing model to serve the entire market efficiently.”

West’s comments hint at why the top semiconductor foundries such as TSMC and Samsung have not jumped into the quantum business.

Canadian quantum chip designer Xanadu is an example of the complexities of manufacturing.

Xanadu uses Taiwanese chip foundry UMC to make thin-film lithium niobate for its quantum processing units as well as other undisclosed foundries to make III-V semiconductors that Xanadu is assembling in Canada, Xanadu COO Rafal Janik told EE Times.

Winning customers

Anderon said it is starting to attract customers.

“Anderon is actively engaging with potential customers across the quantum ecosystem, including fabless processor developers, full system builders, national laboratories and programs, and more,” newly appointed Anderon CEO Mukesh Khare told EE Times. “We believe there is strong demand for a dedicated, U.S.-based quantum wafer foundry and are excited by the interest we’ve seen across the industry.”

Anderon offers specialized wafers supporting high-performance superconducting qubit arrays, quantum input/output signaling, and readout signal chain components, which support a range of quantum architectures, Khare added. The company plans to expand to other quantum chip modalities such as spin qubits, he noted.

While IBM has chosen superconducting qubits as the basis for its quantum computers, rivals are betting on alternatives such as quantum dots, carbon vacancies, or trapped ions to create qubits.

“I would characterize the award as backing the development of a U.S. quantum manufacturing capability rather than making a government bet on IBM’s particular quantum architecture,” West said. “The fact that Anderon is structured as a pure-play foundry and intends to serve the broader quantum ecosystem is important here.”

Quantum computing is reaching a point where improvements in the underlying technology increasingly depend on manufacturing scale, process control, and supply chain access, West said.

“The U.S. is trying to establish domestic capacity in strategically important semiconductor technologies,” West added. “Investing now gives the ecosystem time to develop manufacturing capabilities before demand for large-scale quantum systems becomes significant.”

Quantum chipmakers are likely to increasingly rely on external foundries as the industry moves from research prototypes toward higher-volume production, according to IDC.

“Quantum companies need confidence that their intellectual property and process know-how are protected, while also relying on the foundry for process consistency, yield, and dependable access to capacity,” West said. “As quantum systems scale, that combination of technical capability, manufacturing reliability, and trust will make foundry relationships increasingly strategic.”

data.title: SK Hynix’s Intel Liaisons: What You Need to Know
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

SK Hynix’s Intel liaisons are making waves again. According to Reuters, SK Hynix could lease part of Intel’s chipmaking facility in Ohio, which is currently struggling to be completed. The world’s largest chipmaking complex in Ohio was originally scheduled to begin chip fabrication in 2025, but completion of the site’s two fabs ⁠has since been delayed to 2030 and 2031.

Another scenario suggests SK Hynix could form a joint venture with Intel and major AI hyperscalers to secure a steady supply of increasingly scarce memory chips. However, the Reuters story noted that SK Hynix could also explore other deal structures, and that the talks are exploratory, with no decisions made yet.

Intel declined to comment on the story, calling it speculation. The Santa Clara, California-based chipmaker also reiterated its commitment to continue investing in the Ohio site, a key pillar of the U.S. semiconductor manufacturing strategy.

So, what’s going on? What’s behind this media frenzy? For a start, this isn’t exactly breaking news. There’s been market chatter about SK Hynix acquiring Intel’s Ohio fab, as well as SK Hynix partnering with Intel to help operate the fab instead of taking full ownership.

News reports have also described Intel and SK Hynix exploring initiatives similar to SK Hynix’s HBM and advanced packaging partnership with TSMC. These reports claimed that SK Hynix has been testing the integration of its HBM devices with Intel’s Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB)-based 2.5D packaging technology.

These media reports seemed credible because SK Hynix’s HBM rivals—Micron and Samsung—have also been assessing EMIB’s compatibility and power efficiency for their advanced memory solutions to make a broader push toward diversified packaging solutions amid the tight supply of TSMC’s Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) offerings.

Still, SK Hynix’s Intel liaison seems to paint a picture that’s more politics than business. Start with the U.S. government’s threat to impose more tariffs on tech companies from South Korea and Taiwan if they fail to invest in U.S. manufacturing, and the picture becomes clearer.

More politics than business

The South Korean government is currently in talks with the U.S. over the implementation of a proposed $350 billion investment commitment to Washington to reduce tariffs on South Korean goods. However, a manufacturing arrangement with Intel would be unique in that it would bring the production of advanced memory chips to American soil.

It’s also apparent that the Korean memory duo—Samsung and SK Hynix—is under tremendous pressure to expand production to meet the growing demand for storage in AI designs. However, the South Korean government wants to increase memory chipmaking capacity on its shores to keep the country competitive in the AI race.

On the other hand, the U.S. government, aiming to bolster onshore advanced semiconductor manufacturing, wants to reduce reliance on foreign supply chains, which currently come primarily from Taiwan and South Korea. Micron is the only major company producing advanced memory wafers in the U.S.

SK Hynix chairman Chey Tae-won has been reflecting on this challenge. In July, while speaking to reporters, he acknowledged that SK Hynix faces ⁠enormous pressure to produce more memory chips. “I think we need to build a factory in the United States,” he said. “If possible, I believe we should build it.”

Industry watchers point out that a deal with SK Hynix would ease some of the financial strain on Intel, which is now part-owned by the U.S. government. It will also mark a big win for the U.S. government, which has been ramping up pressure on chipmakers to build fabs in the U.S.

Is the deal imminent?

SK Hynix is investing nearly $4 billion in an advanced packaging facility in West Lafayette, Indiana. This advanced packaging and test facility, dedicated to HBM devices, is scheduled to begin full-scale operations in the second half of 2028.

However, the reported talks between Intel and SK Hynix matter because front-end manufacturing of advanced memory devices such as HBM is strategically important. At this crossroads, SK Hynix must walk a fine line while trying to please both Seoul and Washington.

Nevertheless, the deal seems imminent not because of technology business imperatives, but because of a much larger geopolitical story behind the potential partnership. More details are likely to emerge in the coming days, and EE Times will keep you posted on this technology business soap opera intertwined with geopolitics.

data.title: Smarter Cameras Need More Than Edge AI to Protect Privacy
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

A camera monitoring a distribution center may need to detect a blocked emergency exit, warn when a worker enters a hazardous area, or follow packages through a production flow. None of those tasks require knowing the worker’s identity.

Yet that same camera may need to preserve recognizable evidence if a theft, accident, or intrusion occurs. The challenge for intelligent video systems is therefore not simply to see less; it’s to determine when identity is necessary, suppress it when it’s not, and tightly control the footage when it must remain.

“The idea is not to collect and record more material or data than what’s needed to fulfill the use case,” Mats Thulin, director of AI and analytics solutions at Axis Communications, told EE Times.

Intelligence moves into the camera

Axis is a professional security camera manufacturer, with approximately 5,500 employees and a network of about 90,000 system integration partners. Its cameras increasingly act as real-time sensors rather than passive recording devices.

Thulin described systems that detect people entering hazardous areas, identify missing hard hats, warn of pedestrians near industrial vehicles, monitor blocked exits, and provide early warnings of smoke or overheating equipment. Cameras can also count occupants, track packages, and support manufacturing quality assurance.

“In all of those examples, you blur out people to protect privacy because you’re not interested in recording video of people,” Thulin said.

Axis cameras perform AI analysis locally using the company’s ARTPEC system-on-chip (SoC). According to Thulin, all cameras in the current portfolio are AI-enabled, with deep-learning processing handled directly in the ARTPEC SoC rather than requiring separate dedicated hardware.

Applications such as Axis Live Privacy Shield analyze the stream inside the camera; detect people, faces, or license plates; and replace the relevant pixels before routine video leaves the device. Fixed areas, such as windows overlooking private property, can also be blocked.

For an occupancy application, the camera might send only a count to a dashboard. In a distribution center, it can follow parcels while masking employees. Processing locally also reduces the need to transmit continuous video to the cloud.

“Instead of feeding the full video to a cloud environment where it’s stored somewhere, and you lose track of privacy, the camera can perform the counting and send only the required result,” Thulin said.

But not every camera is used only for counting or process monitoring. Banks, schools, retailers, airports, and transport operators may have legitimate reasons to retain identifiable evidence following an incident.

Thulin described a bank installation in which routine users receive masked video, while the camera also sends an encrypted, unmasked stream to protected storage. Operator and administrator roles can separate routine monitoring from the ability to change privacy settings or retrieve identifiable footage.

“If the use case is to identify a break-in, of course you want to record the person doing an intrusion,” Thulin said. “In those cases, it’s about how you maintain the security of that data.”

Axis also cryptographically signs footage so an organization can demonstrate that it came from a particular camera and was not subsequently altered. Long-term software support, patching, encryption, and access controls are therefore part of the privacy architecture.

In some cases, Axis restricts the device itself. Thulin pointed to acoustic sensors that can detect screams, shouts, or breaking glass but cannot be configured to stream conversations. Privacy is stronger when unnecessary surveillance is technically unavailable rather than merely prohibited by policy.

Privacy risks continue after recording

But even carefully controlled footage can become intrusive when it’s extracted and shared. Pimloc addresses this later stage of the video lifecycle through its Secure Redact platform.

The software uses AI to detect and track faces, heads, bodies, license plates, scene text, and other sensitive details across recorded video. An authorized user can choose which individuals should remain visible, anonymize everyone else, review the results, and generate a separate file for release.

Simon Randall, CEO of Pimloc, gave the example of a school sharing footage of an incident with parents. The parents may need to see what happened to their child but should not receive identifiable video of every other child present.

“The anonymization needs to be irreversible,” Randall told EE Times. “We effectively create a whole new version of the file with that personal information removed. So it’s theoretically impossible to get back to what was there before.”

Users may blur or pixelate faces or replace an entire region with black pixels. Full bodies can be removed when a person’s height, clothing, or surroundings could reveal identity. Secure Redact can also remove names, addresses, financial information, and individual speakers from audio, while stripping metadata that could disclose time or location.

The original is not necessarily destroyed. It may remain in protected storage for evidentiary purposes, while only the redacted version is distributed.

“If you anonymized it at the device, it’s better—it’s more private—because you never capture the stuff to start with,” Randall said. “The question is: Under what circumstances is that useful?”

Pimloc automates tasks that can otherwise be prohibitively slow. Randall cited a customer that required three-and-a-half weeks to manually redact a particularly challenging 20-minute body-camera video. He said Pimloc reduced the review stage to about 15 minutes.

But automation does not eliminate human verification. Real security footage may be grainy, crowded, poorly lit, or captured by a rapidly moving body-worn camera. Users must confirm that every relevant identifier has been found and that the correct people remain visible.

The platform also preserves a record of what was changed. Pimloc hashes the incoming file, logs the redaction process, and hashes the finished version. That chain of custody complements Axis’s camera-level signing.

“The other thing that’s just as important now is being able to prove authenticity and provenance of content,” Randall said. “There’s privacy in not disclosing private information, but the other thing is making sure that what you do disclose is true and accurate.”

Privacy across the lifecycle

Strong privacy can make video more usable rather than less usable. Properly anonymized footage can be shared with parents, citizens, lawyers, operational teams, researchers, or the public without unnecessarily identifying bystanders.

“I would argue that it’s a counterintuitive point, but by having really good privacy, it means you can actually make a lot more use of the data,” Randall said.

Neither company, however, treats edge AI or masking as sufficiently on its own. Cameras can be reconfigured, administrators can misuse access, vulnerabilities can expose streams, and a system installed for safety can gradually expand into employee monitoring or customer profiling.

Cybersecurity, access control, retention limits, auditing, integrator practices, and regulation determine whether the original privacy design survives.

“A lot of people put privacy and security at opposite ends of a continuum,” Randall said. “We need to do both together.”

Security cameras can therefore become more intelligent without necessarily becoming more intrusive. But privacy must extend across the full lifecycle: what the camera captures, what it analyzes, what it transmits, what it stores, who can retrieve it, and what remains visible when it’s shared.

The decisive question is not simply whether AI runs at the edge; it’s whether the system can justify when identity matters, technically suppress it when it does not, and protect the original whenever it must remain.

data.title: Pasqal’s Nasdaq Debut Meets a Risk Reckoning
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Pasqal received an enthusiastic welcome from investors when the French neutral atom quantum computing company began trading on Nasdaq on Aug. 28 after completing a merger with Bleichroeder Acquisition Corp. II.

Bleichroeder was a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), a publicly traded shell company created to identify a private business to merge with and take public; it ultimately selected Pasqal. Bleichroeder shares closed at $9.79 on August 27, the day before Pasqal began trading under its own ticker. After the combination took effect, the stock closed at $19.11 on its first day as Pasqal. The enthusiasm faded quickly. By the following week, the shares were trading at about $8, roughly 58% below their first-day close. They have remained near that level since, closing at $7.77 on September 15.

The decline says little by itself about whether Pasqal’s technology will ultimately succeed. But it illustrates the difficulty investors face in valuing quantum companies that need industrial-scale capital today while much of their commercial opportunity remains in the future.

Pasqal now has roughly $360 million in cash available to pursue that scale-up. According to public filings, the company has seven quantum processing units (QPUs) deployed and three more in production. It reported €16.5 million (~$19 million) in commercial revenue in 2025, up from €3.5 million (~$4 million) in 2024, while the transaction valued Pasqal at $2 billion before the new financing.

Pasqal CEO Wasiq Bokhari agreed to answer EE Times questions about the company’s commercialization plans, capital requirements, and transition to the public markets, but did not follow through with responses.

From physics experiment to product

According to Sean Sullivan, co-founder and CTO of quantum networking company memQ, the hundreds of millions of dollars now being raised by quantum companies reflect a genuine shift in the challenges facing the industry. “It’s about turning what have traditionally been like physics experiments into products that you can actually buy and then use,” he told EE Times.

That means replacing collections of specialized laboratory equipment with integrated systems built around components that can be reliably manufactured, packaged, interconnected, and supplied at scale.

According to Pasqal’s investor materials, its manufacturing facilities in France and Canada can produce up to 13 QPUs annually, subject to full staffing and parts availability. The company also reports that its latest-generation machine has achieved 1,024 trapped atoms.

Sullivan said investment across the quantum sector is increasingly flowing toward fabrication, packaging, integrated control systems, supply chains, and other relatively mundane engineering problems rather than purely fundamental physics. The physics has not disappeared, he cautioned. But the questions are changing from whether quantum systems can work at all toward how to engineer them reliably and economically.

Money helps because it lets companies iterate faster. They can run more fabrication cycles, operate more development systems in parallel, and test more approaches. “It just gets you more shots on goal to engineer around some challenges,” Sullivan said.

But capital cannot make fundamental physical constraints disappear. That leaves investors financing several competing quantum architectures before it’s clear which approaches will prove easiest to scale commercially.

Venture risk in public stock

For Hamiz Awan, founder and CEO of Plutus21 Capital, today’s publicly traded quantum companies look less like conventional public equities and more like venture investments. “Even though these are public companies, it’s just a venture investment,” he told EE Times.

Current financial performance alone cannot explain many quantum company valuations, he said. Investors are instead paying for technical progress, intellectual property, scarce engineering talent, and essentially an option on a potentially enormous future market.

That also means accepting venture-style probabilities: Several companies and architectures may receive substantial financing while only a small number ultimately generate outsized returns. Awan said he believes technology is only part of what is driving money into quantum. Liquidity, momentum, and fear of missing the next major technology cycle after AI are also important.

“Most investors understand momentum,” he said, adding that he doubts most have enough technical knowledge to judge the relative merits and maturity of the competing quantum approaches. Pasqal’s first weeks of trading illustrate how quickly that momentum can reverse.

Public markets also impose a different discipline from private financing. “As soon as you become a public company, if somebody disagrees with you or your projections, they have a very clean way of betting against you,” Awan said. “For the first time, these quantum companies are seeing levered selling pressure from people that are betting against them.”

At the same time, public shares give capital-intensive companies a potentially powerful financing tool. Stock can be used to raise additional capital, compensate employees, or finance acquisitions.

What counts as commercial progress?

If stock market enthusiasm is unreliable, the harder question is what investors should use to measure progress. Philip van den Berge, founder and CEO of stock analysis platform Intrinsiqq, argued that investors should look beyond quantum company partnership announcements and focus on transactions that demonstrate customers are actually paying for and using the technology.

“What I’m mostly looking for is contracts, machines,” van den Berge told EE Times. What matters most, he said, is whether customers actually take delivery and then “buy a second one.”

The repeat sale is particularly significant, he said. A first quantum system may be purchased for experimentation. A customer returning for another suggests the first deployment provided enough value to justify additional spending.

Pasqal’s commercial revenue provides some evidence of movement in that direction. Commercial revenue rose from €3.5 million in 2024 (~$4 million) to €16.5 million (~$19 million) in 2025. Pasqal also reported more than €66 million (~$76.2 million) in booked and awarded business as of March 2026, although the company indicated that figure includes grants.

Despite its falling share price, however, Pasqal remains valued at many times its current sales. At around $8 a share, its market capitalization of roughly $1.7 billion equates to about 89 times its 2025 commercial revenue. That multiple reflects expectations of a much larger future business rather than Pasqal’s present sales.

Capital buys time

The final capital position was also substantially below the level contemplated when the transaction was announced. In March, Pasqal and Bleichroeder projected more than $600 million in gross proceeds, a figure that included existing Pasqal cash and assumed no SPAC redemptions. When the transaction closed on August 27, Pasqal reported approximately $360 million in cash available.

Van den Berge cautioned against estimating how long that money will last simply by comparing it with historical losses. Manufacturing costs and other spending may rise as Pasqal scales, while cash flow is a better measure of capital consumption than accounting losses.

For Awan, the more important question is what Pasqal accomplishes with the money. “A lot of times, the capital that’s raised is honestly just to keep the lights on,” he said.

If companies remain primarily in experimentation mode several years after raising hundreds of millions of dollars, he argued, the capital may have extended their runway without proving that they have scalable businesses.

Pasqal’s share price decline does not settle the question of whether neutral atom quantum computing will succeed. But it does show how difficult public markets find it to price that possibility.

Pasqal now has hundreds of millions of dollars to move its technology toward industrial scale. The harder task is proving that industrial scale can become commercial scale.

data.title: FCC Rule on Optical Connectivity Could Slow AI Race
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The technological trade conflict between the U.S. and China could extend beyond high-end chips. While the initial restrictions focused on advanced semiconductors and the equipment used to produce them, Washington is now eyeing the wider data center infrastructure.

The new strategy is about rack sovereignty. The concept is straightforward: Securing the GPUs is not enough if other components of the networking fabric create potential security or supply chain vulnerabilities. To deal with this, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) issued a new rule last week, “Protecting Against National Security Threats to the Communications Supply Chain Through the Equipment Authorization Program,” affecting the small but important components that convert electricity into light for high-speed data transmission.

The FCC has established compliance dates for the new rule: 

  • March 1, 2027: for online marketplaces that sell their own devices, take title, or have physical access to third-party seller inventory.
  • June 1, 2027: for marketplaces that host third-party listings without physical access/title (must verify FCC ID against the FCC database and collect seller certifications).

The geopolitical weight here comes from an asymmetric dependency. Chinese firms such as Zhongji InnoLight dominate global revenue, but they rely on U.S. cloud giants for their most advanced orders. 

The numbers back up this dominance. According to Counterpoint Research estimates, Zhongji InnoLight, which was added ​to the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies in June, sits at the top of the food chain, commanding roughly 27% of global revenue. They’ve locked in a prime spot supplying the high-end 800G and 1.6T modules that North American cloud giants are currently hungry for.

San Jose, Calif.-based Coherent follows in second with a 17% slice of the pie, while Eoptolink—another Chinese heavyweight with deep ties to U.S. hyperscalers—is catching up fast. Lumentum, also based in San Jose, holds about 6% of the finished module market, though its greater strength lies in supplying the laser components that make these modules work.

Meanwhile, Western companies still rely on Chinese manufacturing for high-volume packaging. In this complex environment, Coherent is emerging as a vital U.S. domestic partner as efforts to build more sovereign infrastructure gain momentum.

Closing the component loophole

The FCC’s move targets what it calls the “component part loophole.” Previously, a device made by a company that was not on the Covered List could still receive FCC authorization even if it incorporated a component produced by a Covered List entity. Under rules adopted by the FCC in July 2026, that loophole is closed. The new rule further clarifies it.

The FCC has redefined “logic-bearing hardware” to include hardware components that process data at high speeds, including optical transceivers. 

Optical transceivers fall under the new rule’s scope because they are physical components that generate and use timing signals or pulses at a rate exceeding 9,000 pulses (cycles) per second and utilize digital techniques.

As a result, if a network device incorporates a covered logic-bearing component made by a company on the blocklist, the whole unit could be denied FCC authorization, potentially limiting its entry into the U.S. market. If optical transceivers fall within the rule’s scope, this could amount to a substantial exclusion of Chinese technology from the core of AI data centers.

Optical transceivers are sometimes considered “dumb” pipes with little security threat, because they merely convert signals and do not run full operating systems suitable for hacking. Yet this is not quite accurate given the speeds needed for modern AI (800G and 1.6T).

Modern modules are complex systems that can include DSPs and firmware. This internal software manages everything from power to data paths. If that firmware is not secure, an attacker could manipulate diagnostics or trigger thermal spikes. In a massive cluster, one faulty module can blind a switch to overheating or inject just enough latency to make a billion-dollar GPU array go idle.

Challenging the symbiotic loop

The problem is that China currently dominates this market. According to Counterpoint Research, China accounts for about 60% of global optical datacom transceiver revenue, with Zhongji Innolight leading the pack. Because U.S. export bans prevent Chinese cloud operators from using the most powerful GPUs, these Chinese manufacturers have little choice but to sell their best 800G and 1.6T modules to U.S. hyperscalers.

“Market share of Chinese companies would be significantly affected as these companies depend on overseas customers—mainly the big U.S. hyperscalers—for more than 90% of their high-value 800G and 1.6T module revenues,” Gareth Owen, associate director of Counterpoint Research, told EE Times.

To dodge the potential ban, many are moving production to Southeast Asia. But if the FCC targets ownership rather than just the factory location, those moves won’t matter. It’s a messy, symbiotic loop: Chinese makers need U.S. DSPs, while U.S. companies need Chinese assembly scale.

Packaging deficit

When the FCC news broke in August, Western suppliers such as Coherent and Lumentum saw their stock prices jump, but analysts were not entirely convinced. Western firms lack the specialized cleanrooms and massive scale to replace Chinese production anytime soon. Last year, McKinsey projected a 40% to 60% shortfall in 800G transceivers through 2027, with 1.6T transceiver shortfalls of 30-40% persisting through 2029.

In response to questions from EE Times, Counterpoint Research argued that the potential ban could have severe consequences for the AI arms race:

  • Capacity deficit: Western competitors such as Coherent and Lumentum have advanced photonic designs, but currently lack the cleanroom capacity, automated packaging infrastructure, and yield scale to absorb Innolight and Eoptolink’s volume within a 12- to 24-month horizon.
  • Cluster turn-up delays: In an AI supercluster, a missing batch of optical transceivers could leave billion-dollar GPU allocations idle. Constraining transceiver imports could delay the commercial turn-up of next-generation 800G/1.6T clusters by multiple quarters.
  • Capital cost escalation: Restricting market supply in a hyper-growth environment could increase bill-of-materials (BOM) costs for hyperscale data centers, forcing cloud operators to pay higher premiums for non-Chinese allocations.

“This would also cause major problems for hyperscalers such as AWS, Google, Meta, and Microsoft, as a lack of optical transceivers potentially lays idle billions of dollars of the latest GPUs,” Owen told EE Times. “Hyperscalers must therefore move quickly to ensure that they have alternative supply chains in place before the ban is enacted—currently expected before the end of 2026, although this may be pushed back a little.”

Potential laser chokepoint

There’s also a raw material crisis. Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston warned that the shortage of indium phosphide (InP), used for the lasers in modules, is more severe than the memory chip crisis. 

Demand has jumped from hundreds of lasers for telecoms to hundreds of millions for AI. Since China controls 70% of refined indium, it could easily retaliate by cutting off the supply of the very lasers Western companies need to build their own alternatives.

To hedge these risks, giants such as Nvidia are stepping in. “With Coherent, we are pioneering next-generation silicon photonics to enable AI infrastructure at unprecedented scale, speed, and energy efficiency,” Nvidia’s Jensen Huang said. 

Coherent CEO Jim Anderson added that the deal highlights his firm’s role as “a key enabler of next-generation AI data center infrastructure.”

Coherent and Lumentum did not respond to EE Times’ requests for comment.

Rise of silicon photonics

This uncertainty is also accelerating the move toward silicon photonics—integrating optics directly onto the chip to skip traditional packaging altogether. Lumilens, which emerged from stealth on Aug. 6 with a $5.51 billion valuation, has begun shipping interconnect solutions to an unnamed hyperscale cloud provider.

“The constraint on AI has shifted from how many GPUs you can buy to how many you can connect,” Lumilens CEO Ankur Singla said. “Hyperscalers need far more optical capacity for the networks they run today, and a path to directly connecting thousands of GPUs together into a single cluster.”

Reconfiguring this global supply chain carries significant risks. The FCC is taking an unprecedented step in the physical layer of internet infrastructure. Still, without sufficient domestic capacity or dependable raw materials, this attempt for greater sovereignty could hinder the very AI leadership that the U.S. is trying to protect.

data.title: India Hardens Its Cyber Defenses
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

When militants launched a terror attack in Pahalgam, a popular tourist destination in Indian-administered Kashmir, in April 2025, India’s government attributed the violence to Pakistani insurgents and responded with Operation Sindoor, a military operation that relied on digital network coordination for precision strikes. In the days that followed, violence escalated between the nations, and while a ceasefire soon ensued, this was not before an explosion of digital attacks on infrastructure and public-facing services—from both sides.

As Lieutenant General Madhavan Unnikrishnan Nair, India’s former National Cyber Security Coordinator and a visiting professor at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar, told EE Times: “Our distributed denial-of-service [DDoS] attacks went up multi-fold and they were all focused on critical infrastructure, like our financial sector.

“During April and May 2025, we had one of the largest DDoS attacks in the world at that point in time,” he added. “Yet our cybersecurity ecosystem was potent enough to hold on, and we survived—none of our services went down.”

But while the DDoS attacks failed to disrupt services, the India–Pakistan conflict reinforced the urgent need to bolster digital defenses. Nair has since spoken out on how the digital domain is now “a primary theater of national security,” and given that India has one of the largest digital public infrastructures in the world, this makes it particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks.

A key issue that the government has been working to address is that India’s infrastructure relies on many legacy systems, installed long before cybersecurity was a significant threat.

Post-Covid and following a rise in digital technology use across India, the government reviewed cybersecurity, implementing network standards for devices based on the role and criticality of each device. By 2021, the Mandatory Testing and Certification of Telecommunications Equipment scheme was in full swing, progressively integrating cybersecurity standards and bringing networking devices, routers, and Passive Optical Network series broadband equipment under compulsory testing.

More recently, telecom-connected IoT equipment has also required regulatory clearances to connect to India’s networks. In April this year, the government formally enacted an absolute mandate on internet-enabled CCTV cameras, requiring all surveillance systems to undergo strict Standardization Testing and Quality Certification cybersecurity testing before being legally sold or imported. “As part of our smart city projects, we’d installed many CCTV cameras to monitor traffic, but we found that many of these cameras were being misused for anti-national activities by both state and non-state actors,” Nair said.

Nair described how a deepening technological alignment between China and Pakistan on network infrastructure integration, AI system development, satellite intelligence cooperation, and other digital applications adds to the rising cyberthreat. “We receive threats from our western and northern geographic borders, and we needed to protect our citizens’ data,” he said.

As IoT becomes more widespread, Nair also highlighted the government’s unease over distinguishing between human- and machine-generated data and understanding the origin of data. “We need to know the source, because otherwise, how do you differentiate between what is lawful and what is unlawful?” he said. “Who will be responsible, who will be attributable, who will be liable—how do you ultimately protect the lives of citizens?

“We need to sit together as a committee of nations and create measures that require a signature or stamp that shows where all data originates—this needs more than one nation,” he added.

Prompted by India’s rapidly expanding IoT infrastructure, the government has started to push more aggressively into edge computing and utility infrastructure, introducing targeted cybersecurity certification to smart electricity meters, vehicle trackers, and feedback devices. “Shutting down a smart meter in one home won’t make a big difference … but smart meters are part of a larger network—could someone shut down an entire geographic region?” Nair said. “Even closed networks can be penetrated through supply chain vulnerabilities—this will affect all of us.

“Today, any device connected to a network is vulnerable … and AI has added to our challenges because it makes manipulating systems so much easier,” he added.

Digital sovereignty

As the challenges mount up, digital sovereignty will become more critical to India’s future cybersecurity. In late 2025, the number of internet users in India tipped beyond 1 billion, second only to China’s gargantuan figure of 1.3 billion and far exceeding the 324 million users in the U.S., according to the October 2025 Global Digital Report from Singaporean consultancy Kepios.

Factor in India’s immense digital infrastructure, which includes Aadhaar, a 12-digit unique identity number for citizens based on residence, biometrics, and demographic data; the Unified Payments Interface, a cash- and card-free instant payment system; and rapid 5G adoption, and it’s clear to see that the scale of its digital footprint demands sovereign control.

Nair highlighted how the government is already acting on legacy software associated with power generation systems, “wrapping around” a layer of cybersecurity protection. “It’s been a difficult concept, but it has been doable,” he said.

However, the former National Cyber Security Coordinator highlighted how his nation’s rise to power hinges on cyber-resilience investment on par with the threat as well as rapid governance reform that matches the adversary’s ability to adapt to technological change. In his recent article, “India’s Digital Front: Cyber Threats, Strategic Vulnerabilities and the Imperative of a Sovereign Digital India,” published by NatStrat, a not-for-profit center for research on strategic and security issues, Nair laid out key priorities for building digital sovereignty in India. These included accelerated development of India’s indigenous semiconductor design and fabrication ecosystem under the India Semiconductor Mission as well as the creation of sovereign cloud infrastructure physically located in India, governed by Indian law, and operated by entities free of foreign government obligations. Regulation of the app ecosystem requiring each application to comply with minimum cybersecurity standards and mandating that every device connecting to any network meets minimum cybersecurity certification norms was also included.

“We need to develop bilateral and multilateral agreements that protect our data—this is where the future should lie,” Nair said. “We also need to understand that the technology landscape is changing so fast today that predictions that we make today may not hold true tomorrow.

“We’ll always be catching up, but I think while technology gives you new challenges, it also gives you opportunities to protect our systems,” he added. “That’s what we should focus on.”

data.title: Ambient IoT: From Battery-Free Promise to Mass-Market Reality

In June, U.S. analyst Precedence Research forecasted a mighty 34.7% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) for the global ambient IoT market, up from $2,450 million this year to $35,780 million in 2035. North America accounted for the highest revenue share of 39% in 2025, and Asia-Pacific is poised for the fastest CAGR of 40.6% between now and 2035.

The robust figures coincide with a glut in ambient IoT investment worldwide. In April, U.S.-based global digital identification manufacturer Avery Dennison invested $75 million in Israeli ambient IoT platform and device provider Wiliot. “We believe in the power of passive Bluetooth Low Energy and the significant opportunity to expand our portfolio with the solutions from Wiliot,” Francisco Melo, Avery Dennison’s president of intelligent labels technologies and digital solutions, said at the time.

The investment followed Norwegian fabless IoT company ONiO’s €5 million Series A funding round to ramp production of its general-purpose ambient IoT microcontroller, just as Australian ambient IoT middleware platform and software development kit provider Embeint raised $500,000 AUD (~$350,000) in pre-seed funds to grow U.S. and European markets. Then in July this year, Belgian ambient energy-harvesting power management IC manufacturer e-peas secured $22 million in financing to scale commercial growth and accelerate international expansion.

E-peas co-founder and CEO Geoffroy Gosset is certain that the ambient IoT energy-harvesting market is at an inflection point, with the tech already reaching markets from smart homes and consumer devices to industry logistics and agriculture. “I think the technology is becoming more and more understood,” he told EE Times. “When we started the company [in 2014], people at trade shows would ask us, ‘What the hell are you doing? What is it used for? Do you believe in that?’

“But now they come to us with projects: They say, ‘I bought this on Mouser or DigiKey, and I’d like to talk to you [about] the next step of our project,’” he said. “These projects are growing very fast.”

Building control

Ambient IoT uses interconnected, battery-less IoT devices that operate autonomously, powered by energy harvesting from light, heat, motion, or radio waves. By removing batteries and maintenance, these devices can be embedded at scale in buildings, supply chains, and warehouses to monitor and control systems such as HVAC and lighting.

For over a decade, industry players from around the world have been developing energy-harvesting tech. For example, U.S.-based Everactive emerged from the Universities of Michigan and Virginia in 2012 to develop battery-free IoT sensor networks, while e-peas was founded in 2014 to develop energy-harvesting PMICs. Dutch semiconductor company Nowi, now owned by Nexperia, launched in 2016 to make energy-harvesting PMICs, while U.S.-based Atmosic was founded in the same year to develop ultra-low-power Bluetooth chips for ambient IoT devices. Wiliot followed in 2017 with battery-free Bluetooth tags and the technology underpinning its ambient IoT tracking platform.

Along the way, industry heavyweights, including Infineon Technologies, Intel, and Qualcomm, have joined the ambient IoT tech sector. As the tech has matured, implementations have emerged, reaching logistics and asset tracking first.

Walmart has already used tens of millions of Wiliot ambient IoT battery-free tags, which harvest RF energy from existing Bluetooth infrastructure to track pallets at more than 500 Walmart facilities. Similarly, the U.K.’s Royal Mail has added the tags to more than 900,000 rolling transit cages, across thousands of vehicles, to report real-time cage locations.

For its part, e-peas has manufactured solar-powered Bluetooth keyboards and battery-free remote controls—an e-peas PMIC lies at the heart of the Google TV G32 remote control. Partners range from photovoltaic manufacturers to wireless IC manufacturers, including Qorvo and Silicon Labs. “Smart buildings are also definitely a growing application for us,” Gosset said. “You can use all kinds of sensors in buildings in windows and doors, fire detectors, presence detectors, smart locks—all of this can use energy harvesting.

“Apart from the big semiconductor firms that are not solely focused on energy harvesting, we are the only pure player left,” he added. “Past competitor Nowi was acquired [by Nexperia], and we acquired [the IP of] Trameto—we don’t want anyone to take the place we have gained over the years.”

Scaling networks

With the technology gaining acceptance, deployments scaling, and the sector edging closer to wider commercialization, industry eyes are turning to networks. Cellular standards organization 3GPP added ambient IoT to its standards toward the end of last year, a definitive first step toward establishing a reliable network infrastructure. Industry leaders, including Atmosic, Infineon, Intel, PepsiCo, Qualcomm, VusionGroup, and Wiliot, also joined forces last year to form the Ambience IoT Alliance (AioTA) to develop standards for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and 5G.

Kamesh Medapalli, SVP and global head of systems, research, and innovation for edge systems at Infineon, said he envisages billions of relatively cheap IoT devices being securely connected. “We see ambient IoT as a strategic technology and are striving to develop standards and enable large-scale, sustainable deployments to make IoT devices using ambient power interoperable and accessible around the globe,” he said.

For this to take place, standards are clearly critical, and according to Medapalli, these will work across global spectrums and security, provide interoperability across hundreds of manufacturing platforms, and co-exist with other wireless protocols. For example, he likened the future interoperability standard to Matter, the connectivity standard designed to enhance interoperability and compatibility amongst smart homes and IoT devices.

“We’ll need a similar standard for ambient IoT to work at scale. … [Work] will start at a regional level and then we’ll continue to harmonize the regions together across the globe,” he said. “Progress so far has been focused on awareness, such as white papers and tech talks at industry events like embedded world.”

While ambient IoT is gaining traction, mainstream rollouts will still take time. But Medapalli anticipates key applications to include predictive maintenance applications for HVAC and lighting systems, inventory tracking in warehouses and farms, and environment monitoring, including humidity and temperature sensing. He expects smart home applications, such as voice-assisted systems and TV remotes, to follow.

Medapalli also highlighted how generative AI, which demands massive streams of real-world data, may use some of the secure anonymous data generated by the ambient IoT devices. “This information could help manufacturers gather anonymous data to make better, easier-to-use products tailored for the users,” he said.

Still, the prospect of widespread ambient IoT use and the data it generates has raised concerns around cybersecurity and information protection. As Spanish telecoms multinational Telefónica pointed out in its recent blog, “Ambient IoT and AI: the fusion enabling intelligent environments,” low-power, ambient IoT devices may have limited capacity to implement robust security protocols, making them vulnerable to attacks.

Medapalli highlighted how the AioTA is “actively” addressing this challenge. “We’re working with other bodies, including the 3GPP, IEEE, and Bluetooth SIG to ensure devices can work together while maintaining security requirements,” he said.

In the meantime, ambient IoT developments are continuing apace. Working with AT&T, Wiliot is scaling the deployment of its tracking tags with the telecom giant’s cellular infrastructure to transmit real-time data over the network, enhancing supply chain visibility. Atmosic and U.S.-based embedded software development and edge AI company embedUR Systems have also launched a management platform for ultra-low-power, real-time tracking of assets in warehouses.

Gosset highlighted how e-peas has developed a dual-source, energy-harvesting PMIC that can collect power from two sources, such as PV cells and thermal energy, and has integrated an extremely low-power coulomb counter into its chipsets to monitor energy consumption and storage. The CEO has also claimed a first with a single-chip PMIC that can harvest energy from indoor and outdoor light sources, targeting remote security cameras, consumer devices such as self-charging headphones and e-readers, and other applications.

“We will keep on developing new product lines and focus on tailoring these to get the right PMICs with the right features at the right price for our target markets,” Gosset said.

“We now have more and more high-performance, low-cost PV cells, while PMICs are being optimized for cost,” he added. “Ambient IoT is moving in the right direction, and I’m fairly convinced that fairly soon, [devices] will be a commodity.”

BENGALURU, India — AI in manufacturing is moving beyond isolated proofs of concept, but Indian medium- and small-scale manufacturers face a more fundamental hurdle in the form of inconsistent data, legacy equipment, and the absence of standard operating models.

At last week’s Electronics City Industries Association (ELCIA) Tech Summit 3.0, industry experts argued that scaling AI across manufacturing will depend less on sophisticated models and more on plant-level data, contextual knowledge, and collaboration between manufacturers and technology providers.

In her opening address, Nandini B, chairperson of ELCIA and director of operations at TESCOM Electronics, said the broader manufacturing ecosystem needs to participate in the technology transition.

“Manufacturing today is becoming more sophisticated with AI, automation, advanced electronics, sensors, and whatnot,” she said. “So, small and micro enterprises cannot afford to watch this transformation from the sidelines. They must be a part of it.”

For manufacturers, however, the immediate challenge is not simply adopting AI but ensuring that the systems, data, and processes needed to support it are in place.

Aditi Sharma, president and chief manufacturing excellence officer at Uno Minda, said AI has already moved beyond a nice-to-have capability in manufacturing operations. Uno Minda operates 72 plants making 175 different product types, with some facilities dating back 50 years.

“I am sitting in a space where I am questioning whether I should incorporate AI today or should I do it tomorrow,” Sharma said.

The question, she said, is whether manufacturers should continue with conventional plants because of the availability of human labor in India, or whether human-intensive manufacturing could eventually become a constraint on agility and the adoption of new technology.

Sharma pointed to repetitive operations and the number of physical touches involved in manufacturing as areas where AI can be applied. She added that its deployment also depends on the availability of data and clear ownership.

“We need data, a large amount of data,” she said. “We need the right decision-making, and then we need the correct ownership.”

Ravi Ramarao, founder of Mexo Technologies, said the data challenge began at the machine level. Manufacturing equipment, including modern machines, does not necessarily generate data in a standardized format, making it difficult to directly apply AI across different systems.

Manufacturers need to acquire machine data, combine it with production data, understand production patterns and cycles, and then begin generating recommendations, he said.

“This needs time,” Ramarao said. “Sometimes it varies from three months to six months to understand all the things that are happening in the company and move to an autonomous system, where the AI can make decisions.”

He also cautioned against treating AI models as transferable solutions. “Each organization has its own operating context, which means that data from one organization cannot simply be used to train a model for another,” he said. “That makes contextual data more useful than a sophisticated model that lacks the appropriate data.”

The challenge becomes more pronounced when manufacturers try to replicate a successful proof of concept across multiple plants.

Sharma said proofs of concept are often conducted in controlled environments with the right data, machines, and people. The conditions can be very different at other plants, where data may still be collected manually, and operators may not have experience with digital systems.

“All manufacturing plants in an organization are not at the same level; they have different levels of data,” she said. “Some of them have manual data while others work with digital data, making it difficult to achieve the same results everywhere.”

She said manufacturers should consider replication before beginning a proof of concept, rather than treating it as a separate exercise after the initial project has succeeded.

The experts also distinguished between existing factories and new manufacturing facilities. K. Bhavani Shankar, head of operations, D&M&C, Yaskawa India, said AI could be introduced into existing facilities without completely redesigning them, as much of the equipment installed in recent decades is already capable of connecting to external systems.

“Maybe the equipment, which has been used from 2000 onwards, almost all is ready to connect to the external environment,” Shankar said. “So there, only small changes may be required.”

New factories, however, offer an opportunity to incorporate AI from the outset rather than adapting older equipment and processes later.

Shankar also said the potential of AI extends beyond productivity to quality, resilience, and changes in manufacturing processes.

“If you look at it, the real opportunity of AI, I personally see, is bigger than productivity itself, extending to quality, resilience, and a possible redesign of manufacturing operations and processes,” he said.

Ramarao said the technology should ultimately remain tied to the manufacturing problem it is intended to address. Technology teams can provide the technical foundation, but the relevant business function needs to define the problem.

For Indian medium and small-scale manufacturers, the discussion goes beyond choosing an AI model. The more immediate task is to make different plants, machines, data systems, and operating practices capable of supporting AI technology. Without that foundation, a successful proof of concept may remain just a proof of concept, rather than a solution that can be scaled across the factory network.

Architect Labs is building a platform that lets “anybody” design a custom chip, co-founder Ebrahim Hussain told EE Times in an exclusive interview. Supporting that claim, the startup company has built its prototype Redwood chip on an FPGA in record time.

“Redwood is the first demonstration that is saying this flow works,” Hussain said. “We can actually take something from idea to at least a proof-of-concept. I don’t think you can get any quicker than two weeks.”

That speed includes success on the first batch of test chips from a foundry, known as “A0” silicon. Architect Labs has been using TSMC’s wafer shuttle service that allows multiple chip designs to share a single mask set and production run.

“It’s getting very difficult to build complex A0 silicon on the first shot,” Hussain noted. “We want to help chip companies make it faster but [also] make their development higher quality. The end goal is that A0 goes into full production for our partners.”

Hussain, now 20, skipped high school to study engineering physics at the University of British Columbia before working briefly as a chip designer for Apple and Tesla and joining Stanford University in 2025 as a visiting researcher. He started Architect Labs in July 2025 with co-founder Aaditya Subedi, 19, who today leads a team of 25 people engaged in machine learning, hardware and software engineering, including chip veterans with 20 to 30 years of experience per person.

“I worked for Apple, I worked for Tesla,” Hussain said. “I was on the architecture team and saw how long these cycles really were. It felt like AI would have a big impact on the chip design cycle, but at the same time, it felt like the approach that many people were taking in terms of using AI was not really that potent, it didn’t really feel like it could change much.”

Architect Labs said its technology lets people provide inputs to an AI system that can take over the design and verification of a chip.

“It can test the firmware stack, how the software will interact with the chip,” Hussain said. “It’s very orthogonal to how the traditional verification flow is. Redwood is our first test that is showing this verification technique scales, and we can build complex chips with it.”

The company has built internal blocks and intellectual property for Redwood, which Architect Labs uses as its own training data to recursively improve models.

The company used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 as a primary frontier benchmark for the development of Architect Labs’ models.

“We’ll be releasing a future post about how we’ve gotten our models to actually beat whatever the frontier is providing, which is exciting,” Hussain said.

More creators

OpenAI’s Jalapeño and Amazon’s Trainium demonstrate that more people can create a high-performance chip that’s as good as any inference silicon, Steve Jang, founder of Kindred Ventures and an investor in Architect Labs, told EE Times.

“There’s a serious opportunity to open up this market,” Jang added. “Architect Labs has an opportunity to be analogous the way Claude Code is to software.” In Architect Labs’ case, the company is using AI to slash chip design time.

One notion is that even with a reduced design team, lead time, and capital needs, a project can get halfway to a “productionized” chip in a few weeks, Jang said.

“That’s really cool,” he noted. “Because then you’re making go/no-go decisions with capex and time and resources, having something that you’ve at least been able to test on an FPGA and then run something better than simulations. It would take you a year to two, three years to do that before.”

Customers

Hussain didn’t name customers but said Architect Labs is working with partners to design “some of the most complex ASICs in the world, full-reticle networking switches to bulky chiplets, many different things.” He added, “That’s really our sweet spot: the advanced design nodes. Over time, we’ll start to build more complex ASICs that are built for different purposes than just edge inference.”

The company will announce business engagements soon, including startups, Fortune 500 companies and big chip names, according to Hussain.

“The first instances you see are the model labs,” Hussain said. “They’re the first people with the capital and the demand where it makes sense to build their own chips. As AI grows from the data center to the physical world, we’ll have wearables, robotics, humanoids, self-driving vehicles, all applications that will demand custom chips. Those companies building in those spaces are the ones we want to partner with.”

Hussain has met companies that know workloads very deeply and are buying chips but are starting to think about having their own silicon roadmap.

“If I built a custom chip, what would be the performance gains, the power gains, all of these things?” Hussain asked.

Circumventing EDA

Architect Labs aims to accelerate chip design by circumventing much of the EDA process.

“The bottleneck with traditional EDA is let’s say I have 100 agents working on different parts of a chip,” Hussain said. “It’s difficult to pull together 100 commercial EDA licenses. We take a hybrid approach where around 90% of the verification happens without a commercial simulator. We use some of our own tricks, our own simulators, different technologies we’ve built, and then we use traditional EDA for the sign-off, making sure that this is going to pass all the regression tests.”

Regression tests are automated verification checks that run whenever hardware description code, such as Verilog or VHDL, changes.

Architect Labs doesn’t necessarily expect chip design jobs to become obsolete.

“The chip engineers that we do have in the industry are very supply-constrained,” Hussain said. “With the technology we’re building, we believe more engineers will be able to own more complicated blocks. You’ll need fewer engineers per project, but you’ll now have more projects. Silicon roadmaps will become more aggressive.”

Competition

Architect Labs isn’t alone. Competitors include ChipAgents and Ricursive. ChipAgents announced in September that Andes Technology, a supplier of RISC-V processor IP, cut a processor customization task from 8.5 weeks to six weeks. Ricursive founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini are former Google Brain employees who designed AlphaChip, an AI tool that generates a chip layout in hours. EDA tools provider Synopsys last year said it uses AI agents to “tame” the complexity of chip design.

Jang is betting on Architect Labs.

“The most important thing is, EDA companies don’t want you to solve your problems super-fast,” Jang said. “They want you to spend money, they want you to use their consulting services.”
